items.title: The People Who Became Wildlife
items.summary:
W hat might it be like to be a bird? 

Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles.  

“Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. 

Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock 
 A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. 

First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says. The guide asks people to not immediately categorize or explain what they are experiencing, but to simply notice. 

Once Lawy began trying to inhabit the bird’s perspective, the romantic notion of freedom disappeared. The bird needs shelter, rough…
items.t: The People Who Became Wildlife

items.title: When homeowners saw a student waiting too close to traffic, they built a cozy bus stop reading nook
items.summary:
Florida-based teachers Maren and David Douglass first noticed her on their doorbell camera . While at the hospital for David’s cancer treatment, the couple noticed their home security camera captured a middle schooler sitting on the ground at the edge of their driveway every morning. The school district had made the end of their driveway her bus stop, and with no sidewalk, she waited too close to the road.

They ordered her a bench.

The camera caught her reaction the first morning she saw it. “It was just the cutest reaction, her little jumps, and it just got sweeter from there,” Maren recently told People .

Not long after, a note showed up.

“Hello, this is from the kid that waits for the bus at your house,” it read. “Thank you so much for putting that bench there! Now I don’t have to worry about dirt and bugs, I appreciate it a ton!”

The couple wrote back, and a correspondence started. She became “Bus Kid.” They signed off as “The Bench People.” Notes and small gifts went back and forth at the end of the driveway, and when they learned she loved to read, they put a little free library next to the bench and stocked it with books. Then, other kids in the neighborhood started borrowing from it too.

Maren, who posts on TikTok as @teacherandtraveler , has been documenting it all in a series she calls “ The Adventures of Bus Kid ,” and the videos have pulled in millions of views. Eventually, the two sides met face to face at the end of the driveway, when Maren was home for the afternoon drop-off.

The couple has since turned the whole thing into a self-published children’s…
items.t: When homeowners saw a student waiting too close to traffic, they built a cozy bus stop reading nook

items.title: Scientists say a slight change in one of your senses may signal Alzheimer’s 10 years in advance
items.summary:
We all misplace our keys on occasion. Or draw a blank on why we walked into a room.  Or forget the name of the movie  we saw last week. Naturally, those little mental lapses can trigger a fleeting wave of panic. Understandably, we sometimes worry that our minds are starting to slip.  Is our age catching up to us faster than expected ? Or are we experiencing something more worrisome,  like the early stages of dementia ?

The latest groundbreaking medical research suggests the earliest warning signs of cognitive decline might not start with your memory at all, but with your ears. If you have noticed subtle changes in your hearing lately, it might be worth closer attention.

Hearing changes as an early biological warning bell 

Recent scientific findings from the University of Oulu and the University of Eastern Finland have shed incredible new light on how Alzheimer’s disease and other dementia related conditions develop over time. The research shows that specific hearing issues—including persistent tinnitus and nerve-related hearing loss—frequently serve as early biological red flags. In fact, individuals who later develop dementia are significantly more likely to report hearing difficulties six to ten years before cognitive decline ever appears on anyone’s radar.

In some cases, researchers found that auditory changes can manifest up to fifteen years before memory issues surface. Why would our ears give clues about our brain health? Scientists have proposed a few compelling theories to explain this surprising connection.

One major possibility points to neurodegenerative…
items.t: Scientists say a slight change in one of your senses may signal Alzheimer’s 10 years in advance

items.title: Families are adding a mischievous twist to Thanksgiving with the ‘secret mission’ game
items.summary:
Thanksgiving is almost here. The holiday that brings us family, football, and a delicious  homemade feast that has some of us unbuttoning our pants before dessert is truly one of the best of the year. 

But traditional  family gatherings  can sometimes get a little predictable. Conversations circle the same old topics. Awkward silences inevitably fill the room between dinner and dessert. Relating to relatives you don’t see as often can feel a little weird. 

Traditional Turkey Day decor. Photo credit: David Whelan/Wikimedia Commons 

Thankfully, social media is introducing a brilliant new way to shake things up. Posts started popping up online a year ago showing families playing a hilarious prank called the “secret mission” game. You can find professionally made game kits online , or prepare each mission yourself in advance. It turns the standard holiday gathering into a live-action game of stealth and mischief.

How the ‘secret mission’ game works 

The concept is wonderfully simple and easy to set up. Before the big meal begins, family members pull secret slips of paper listing quirky prompts as “missions.” The goal is to pull off each mission as smoothly as possible.

The mission must be completed before the night ends; the clock starts when appetizers are served and stops after dessert. The real trick is to accomplish your mission without anyone catching on.

The fun lies entirely in keeping a straight face while executing your absurd task. Imagine sitting across from your uncle while he’s clearly trying to complete a bizarre objective. It turns a standard dinner table…
items.t: Families are adding a mischievous twist to Thanksgiving with the ‘secret mission’ game

items.summary:
The Twilight Zone television series made its mark by prompting audiences to examine controversial social issues through the backdoor of science fiction and mystery. One of the most compelling examples, which remains perfectly relevant today, is the 1960 classic “Eye of the Beholder.”

The episode features a woman with her head wrapped in gauze who has undergone her eleventh surgery for her “deformed” face—the final surgery allowed by the totalitarian government. If the surgery is deemed unsuccessful, she will be banished to a ghetto for people with similar deformities. The gauze removal reveals a classically beautiful woman, but the surgery is declared unsuccessful. Then we see that everyone around her—doctors, nurses, government agents—all have deformed pig faces.

Here’s the big reveal:

On November 11, 1960, CBS aired ‘The Twilight Zone’ episode ‘Eye of the Beholder,’ in which a woman lying in a hospital bed with her head wrapped in bandages awaits the outcome of her 11th and final state-approved surgery, a last-ditch attempt to make her look ‘normal’ in a… pic.twitter.com/DSfbK5aHdh 

— RetroNewsNow (@RetroNewsNow) November 11, 2026 

The pressure to conform to a uniform standard of ‘beauty’ 

The woman was beautiful by human standards, but she didn’t conform to pig-face standards, so she was considered hideous and banished. The audience watches this woman who believes she’s ugly because she should have a deformed pig face. She believes it. They believe it. Everyone believes it. 

Everyone except the audience. It’s been 66 years, and the core message still hits…

items.title: Ever walk into a room and instantly forget why you’re there? Psychology says blame the doorway.
items.summary:
You walk into a room knowing you had a plan, but now, somehow, that plan is gone without a trace. You’re left feeling crazy as you ask yourself, “ What did I come in here for? ”

If this happens to you regularly, there may be a surprisingly simple explanation . Thankfully, it has nothing to do with a failing memory or a poor attention span.

Woman trying to remember. Photo credit: Canva 

Psychologists have been studying this phenomenon for years. In a series of experiments, researchers at the University of Notre Dame found that people had more trouble remembering information after passing through a doorway than after traveling the same distance without crossing one. The effect showed up in both virtual and real-world environments.

The answer may lie in how our brains organize moments in our lives. We don’t experience everything as one continuous stream. Instead, we naturally divide what we’re doing into separate events. Getting dressed can be one event. Making breakfast can be another. Starting work can become another, and so on.

Psychologists call this process ‘ event segmentation ‘ 

Those transitions from one event to another are called event boundaries . A location change is a common example, and that’s where the doorway comes into play. Crossing into another room gives your brain a pretty obvious signal that the situation has changed. When that happens, information from the previous event can become harder to retrieve, particularly when something else is competing for your attention.

As our brains update their mental model of what’s happening, this “reset” feels a…
items.t: Ever walk into a room and instantly forget why you’re there? Psychology says blame the doorway.

items.title: We asked people what they enjoy that other people don’t understand. One answer ruled them all.
items.summary:
Some people have quirky hobbies and interests that others might find odd, so when we asked our Upworthy audience on Facebook , “What’s something that you really enjoy that other people can’t seem to understand?” and over 1,700 people weighed in, it wasn’t too surprising. Some people shared things like housework , cleaning and laundry, which a lot of people see as chores. Others shared different puzzles or forms of art they like doing, and still others shared things like long car rides or grocery shopping .

But what was surprising was the one answer that dominated the list of responses. It came in various wordings, but by far the most common answer to the question was “silent solitude.”

A man sits quietly by the water. Photo credit: Canva 

Here are a few examples:

“Feeling perfectly content, when I’m all alone.” 

“Being home. Alone. In silence.” 

“That I enjoy being alone and my soul is at peace in the silence. I don’t need to be around others to feel content, and it takes me days to recharge from being overstimulated after having an eventful day surrounded by others.” 

“Enjoying your own company. Being alone isn’t isolating oneself. It’s intentional peace and healthy… especially for deep feelers/thinkers.” 

Spending time by ourselves is something some of us relish, while some of us hate being alone. Naturally, this points to the common theory of introversion vs. extraversion , but in some ways, that’s overly simplistic. Even the most peopley people among us can enjoy some quality alone time, and not all introverts see time alone as truly enjoyable. (It might be…
items.t: We asked people what they enjoy that other people don’t understand. One answer ruled them all.

items.title: In 1973, the Bee Gees sang an unplugged medley tribute to the Beatles. It’s gorgeous.
items.summary:
By 1973, the Bee Gees ’ career had hit a low. After a series of hits in the late 1960s and early 1970s, including “To Love Somebody,” “How Can You Mend a Broken Heart,” and “I Started a Joke,” the band was in a rut. Their latest album, Life in a Tin Can , and single “Saw a New Morning” sold poorly, and the band’s popularity declined. 

On August 10, 1973, the Gibb brothers (Barry, Robin, and Maurice) appeared on The Midnight Special, a late-night TV show that aired on Saturday mornings at 1 a.m. after The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson. Given the lukewarm reception to their recent releases, the Bee Gees decided to change things up and play a medley of hits from their idols, The Beatles, who had broken up three years before.

The performance, which featured five of the Fab Four’s early hits, including “If I Fell,” “I Need You,” “I’ll Be Back,” “This Boy,” and “She Loves You,” was a stripped-down, acoustic performance that highlighted the Bee Gees’ trademark harmonies.

“When you’ve got brothers singing, it’s like an instrument that nobody else can buy. You can’t go buy that sound in a shop. You can’t sing like The Bee Gees because when you got family members singing together, it’s unique,” Noel Gallagher, who sang with his brother Liam in Oasis, said according to Far Out . 

From folk harmonies to disco kings 

A year later, the Bee Gees performed in small clubs , and it looked like their career had hit a dead end. Then, at the urging of their management, the band began to move in a new direction, incorporating soul, rhythm and blues, and a new, underground musical style…
items.t: In 1973, the Bee Gees sang an unplugged medley tribute to the Beatles. It’s gorgeous.

items.title: One simple word makes children 30 percent more likely to cooperate. It works on adults, too.
items.summary:
Human psychology really isn’t that complicated, if you think about it. Everybody wants to see themselves in a positive light . That’s the key to understanding Jonah Berger’s simple tactic that makes people 30% more likely to do what you ask . Berger is a marketing professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania and the bestselling author of “Magic Words: What to Say to Get Your Way.”

Berger explained the technique using a Stanford University study involving preschoolers. The researchers messed up a classroom and made two similar requests to groups of children ages 3 to 6 to help clean up.

One group was asked, “Can you help clean?” The other was asked, “Can you be a helper and clean up?” The kids who were asked if they wanted to be a “helper” were 30% more likely to want to clean the classroom. The children weren’t interested in cleaning but wanted to be known as “helpers.”

Turning actions into identities 

Berger calls the reframing of the question as turning actions into identities .

“It comes down to the difference between actions and identities. We all want to see ourselves as smart and competent and intelligent in a variety of different things,” Berger told Big Think (video below). “But rather than describing someone as hardworking, describing them as a hard worker will make that trait seem more persistent and more likely to last. Rather than asking people to lead more, tell them, ‘Can you be a leader?’ Rather than asking them to innovate, can you ask them to ‘Be an innovator’? By turning actions into identities, we can make people much more…
items.t: One simple word makes children 30 percent more likely to cooperate. It works on adults, too.

items.title: A man who wanted to ‘see music’ paired a piano with bioluminescent algae. It’s magical to watch.
items.summary:
Music is meant to be heard and not seen, right? Sure, we can watch musicians play instruments , and we can see music notation on paper . But that’s not the same as seeing music itself. 

A young man named He Tongxue from HTX Studio, a team of DIY innovators from Hangzhou, China, wanted to be able to “see music.” He had just started learning piano and felt like the visible dimension was missing. There are plenty of computer programs that create digital visual effects with music, of course. But the goal was to make music visible in real life.

View this post on Instagram 

It took the studio three years, four prototypes, and endless tests to come up with just the right combination of elements. They wanted something that would rise from the piano and light up when the keys were pressed.

Their first idea went up in smoke 

“Our first thought was smoke,” he said. They figured they could line up smoke machines that would be triggered by the piano keys and use lasers to light up the smoke as it rises.

The studio built a prototype, and at first, it looked pretty cool. But after a few minutes of playing, the cool factor wore off. He later described it as “a disaster.”

“The smoke drifts everywhere,” he said. “You can’t tell which light matches which note. It feels like a genie is coming out. And after a while, it feels like someone is barbecuing inside the piano.” 

They wanted the smoke to rise in chunks, like solid musical notes, instead of spreading out. That led them to the idea of vortex rings. Essentially, they could make smoke rings that would give the visible “notes” more…
items.t: A man who wanted to ‘see music’ paired a piano with bioluminescent algae. It’s magical to watch.

items.title: Can Barbershops Turn Trust Into Better Health for Black Men?
items.summary:
I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. 

“It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says.  

The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” 

Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji 
 That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives.  

Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how…
items.t: Can Barbershops Turn Trust Into Better Health for Black Men?

items.title: Maui Is Becoming a Living Laboratory for Regenerative Tourism
items.summary:
O n August 8, 2023, fast-moving wildfires swept through several parts of West Maui. The town of Lahaina, which holds a deep place in Hawaiian history and once served as the capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom, suffered the greatest devastation: Most of its buildings were destroyed, and thousands of residents were displaced. 

The disaster exposed vulnerabilities that had been building long before the flames, from a shortage of affordable housing and dependence on tourism to questions around land use, water access and food security. 

The post Maui Is Becoming a Living Laboratory for Regenerative Tourism appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .
